translations.text: Thus a wise father, a man prudent of mind, old in the virtues of men, taught his noble son with wise words, so that he would prosper well: "Always do what is good; your deeds will serve you well;

God will always be to you lord and helper in every good thing, and an enemy to the other, the one of worse deeds. Hope for the better for yourself; carry this out with zeal always, as long as you live.
Love your father and mother with your heart, and every kinsman, if he holds the Lord dear.
Always be respectful to your elders and fair of speech to them, and keep your teachers dear in your heart and mind, those who most eagerly urge you toward good."
The wise father addressed his son again a second time: "Hold to this with zeal!

Do not commit crime, and never allow wickedness to your friend or kinsman, in case the Lord accuses you of being a witness to the sin. He will repay you with punishment, just as he repays the others with prosperity."

A third time the thoughtful man taught his son from the thoughts of his heart: "Never, through all your long life, make a habit of keeping company with a worse man in any counsel [?], but always take for yourself one who is wise in counsel as a companion for talk and teaching. Let it go with power as it may."
A fourth time the father again taught his beloved son that he should remember this: "Do not betray a special friend, but always keep faith with him with proper courtesy.
Carry this out with zeal, so that you never become false to your friend."

A fifth time the father again began to teach his son with the thoughts of his heart: "Guard yourself against drunkenness and foolish words, wickedness in the mind and lies in the mouth, anger and envy and the love of a woman.
For the man who goes off into the love of a woman, a strange maiden, will often have to go about in shame.
There is always the prospect of sins there, of hateful disgrace, long enmity with God, and overflowing boastfulness. Always be wise in speech, wary of desire, a guardian of your words."

A sixth time the loving father again began to teach his son with kindly thought: "Learn carefully what is good and what is evil, and always tell them apart with a sharp mind in your heart, and always choose the better for yourself.
The choice is always set before you. If your mind is good, wisdom dwells within, and you clearly know what evil is. Hold out against it with courage, and always cherish good in your spirit."

A seventh time the father, the wise man, taught his son and told the young one many things: "A wise man seldom rejoices without sorrow, just as a fool seldom [drymeð ?] in sorrow over his future, unless he knows of a feud.
A man firm in wisdom must think in his breast and be careful in speech, not loud in clamour."

An eighth time the old father began to admonish his son with gentle words: "Learn teaching that is fit to be learned, train yourself in wisdom, hold the Creator of hosts as your hope, and the memory of the saints, and always truth for victory, when you say anything."

A ninth time the old man spoke; the old sage told his son many things: "There are not many people now who are willing to keep the ancient writings, but their mind decays, their courage cools, and the nation grows idle;
they think nothing of it, though they do wrong against the Lord's command. Many will pay for it with the torment of the soul.
But let your mind keep the ancient writings and the Lord's judgments from now on, which men here in every nation let fall away further than would be right for themselves."

A tenth time, full of grievous sorrows, the old man again began to teach his son: "He who, out of love for his soul, always guards himself in his heart against sins of word and deed, and does what is true, makes use of wisdom;
every one of his gifts will be increased by God, abundant in power, when he flees wickedness.
Never let anger, rising high in your heart, overpower you and defile the depths with a surge of fierce words, but a man guards himself against that in a steadfast mind.
A man must be firm in wisdom and moderate, prudent of mind, sharp in his thoughts, eager for wisdom, so that he may win prosperity among men.
Do not be too ready to find fault, nor double-tongued, and do not let men seem too contemptible in your mind, but be kindly; carry a heart light in its thoughts in your breast.
So, my son, remember the wise father's teaching, and always keep yourself from sins."
